items.situation: The March date is fixed. Say it.
tips: We are opening the Austin site in March.
Fixed arrangement, so the present continuous.

items.situation: Eight hires done before June arrives. Say it.
tips: By June we will have hired eight of the eleven.
Future perfect for a finish line.

items.situation: You are deciding right now to send the job descriptions. Say it.
tips: I will send them to counsel by Thursday.
Will, because the decision is happening as you speak.

items.situation: Texas first, then California -- decided last month. Say it.
tips: We are going to open Texas before California.
Going to, because the plan predates this conversation.

items.situation: Explain in one sentence why the ramp-up is not about recruiting.
tips: The constraint is certification, and the training slots are booked a quarter ahead.
Name the real constraint, not the visible one.

items.situation: Say the difference between Texas and California in one sentence.
tips: They are two jurisdictions, not two offices.
Jurisdiction is the word that stops people copying the contract across.

listenings.text: The mistake people from outside the United States make is to think of us as one jurisdiction. We are fifty, plus the federal layer on top, plus cities that make their own rules about pay and about what you may ask a candidate. So the honest answer to almost every question you will ask me is, it depends where. Take notice. There is no statutory notice period in most states, which surprises everybody from Latin America and from Europe. Take non-competes. Routine in Texas, generally unenforceable in California, and the federal position has moved twice in three years. Take pay transparency. In Colorado and in New York you must put a salary range in the advertisement, and in other states you may not even ask what somebody earned before. What I tell every new client is the same thing. Do not build one process. Build one process and a compliance column, and put the state at the top of every page.

We told the board the site would be at full capacity in six weeks and it took seven months. I want to be precise about where the time went, because it was not where anybody expected. Recruiting was not the problem. We filled nine of the eleven roles inside two months. What we had not planned for was that none of the nine could work unaccompanied for another four months, because the certification is site specific and the training slots are booked a quarter ahead. Nobody asked that question, including me. The second thing is that we were running two payrolls in two states with one person who had only ever run one, and by month three she was doing nothing else. If I did it again I would say seven months at the start and I would take the argument in week one, when it costs an uncomfortable meeting, instead of in month four, when it costs your credibility.
